transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-13
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Aaron Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Lumina Head of Platform), Jin Park (Infra), Eliot Rees (ML Eng)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping call to align on capacity sizing for Lumina's recommendation engine, discuss reserved GPU commit + burst capacity, define success criteria and benchmark plan, identify fallback policies for service degradation. Action items and timings agreed at end.

[00:00] Aaron Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Are we good on audio?
[00:12] Maya Lopez: Yep good here. Thanks Aaron, Samira. We wanted to lock down what a POC would look like for serving our recommendation transformer at low-latency, with reserved gpus but the ability to burst.
[00:30] Samira Khan: Great. Quick intro from our side, I'm Samira, run platform performance for Redwood. Aaron will drive commercial, I'll drive the technical sizing and benchmarks.
[00:45] Jin Park: Quick context from our side: production traffic is about 1800 peak rps across 6 priority routes, 95th percentile latency target under 120ms for ranked responses. We currently run mixed A100 and A10 GPUs in house so we're sensitive to cost.
[01:10] Eliot Rees: On the model side it's a 13B transformer, avg prompt length ~120 tokens, we do caching for repeated prefixes, but cold-start token counts can be heavy.
[01:30] Samira Khan: OK that's helpful. Two quick clarifications: when you say 1800 rps is that aggregate inference calls or user-facing sessions?
[01:42] Jin Park: Aggregate inference calls to the ranker endpoint. About 40% of those are short context, 60% heavy where KV cache helps.
[01:54] Aaron Patel: For the POC, what are your success criteria? Maybe define cost target, latency SLO, and rollout window?
[02:05] Maya Lopez: Yes, main thing is proof we can hit 95th <120ms at 75% of production traffic during the week-long pilot, and show predictable unit cost within 15% of our current infra. Also we need auditability for requests for compliance folks.
[02:25] Samira Khan: Compliance wise Redwood Dedicated supports audit logs + KMS integration; we can surface request-level cost breakdown in Redwood Console. We'll include SOC 2 detail in the security packet.
[02:40] Elias (typo on speaker attribution appears) Speaker 5: mm-hm
[02:45] Aaron Patel: Good. On capacity we typically propose a reserved commit sized to cover baseline steady-state QPS and then configure burst pools for traffic spikes. For your numbers, initial rough plan: reserve enough GPU capacity for ~1200 rps steady with autoscaling headroom to burst to 2400 rps via burst pool. That gives margin for spikes.
[03:10] Jin Park: Can you explain how burst works — is it pre-warmed? What about cold start latencies?
[03:18] Samira Khan: Burst capacity can be a warm pool (reserved but inactive) or an on-demand burst into public capacity. Warm pools keep model shards loaded and KV cache warm, minimizing cold-starts. On-demand bursts will have slightly higher cold-starts; we typically route low-priority traffic there or use fallback models.
[03:35] Eliot Rees: Fallback models? Like a smaller quantized model when capacity is constrained?
[03:40] Samira Khan: Exactly. Redwood supports model variants — e.g., a 13B fp16 model as primary and a 6B quantized variant for fallback. We also support automatic policy-based routing: latency-first routes to primary, cost-first routes to cheaper variant.
[03:57] Maya Lopez: We're in a regulated vertical, so data residency and audit are hard requirements. Can the burst to public capacity be prevented for sensitive traffic?
[04:07] Samira Khan: Yes, for sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated with private-only burst or to block publicburst and only use warm reserved pools. On Redwood Private we can enforce no public egress. We'll document the policy options.
[04:20] Aaron Patel: Commercially that maps to two scenarios: 1) Reserved + warm burst pool (higher commit, lower burst ed cost), 2) Reserved + on-demand public burst (lower commit, higher per-use burst cost). We'll model both.
[04:36] Jin Park: How do you size reserved GPU counts? What metrics do you need from us?
[04:44] Samira Khan: Ideally: qps histogram (5m buckets), distribution of sequence lengths, tokenization breakdown, percent cache hits vs cold, target concurrency per GPU for your model family, and any tail-latency constraints. From those we run a capacity simulator to propose GPU counts and batching knobs.
[05:05] Eliot Rees: We can export a 7-day trace from staging with tokens and timestamps. We'll anonymize user ids.
[05:13] Aaron Patel: Perfect. That will let us produce a few commit scenarios. We'll include a scenario that hits your 95th p95 <120ms goal while keeping cost within 15% of current.
[05:25] Maya Lopez: Benchmarks — do you run ones that reflect cold starts? We care about degradation modes not just steady-state.
[05:32] Samira Khan: Yes our POC benchmarks include steady-state QPS, ramp tests (2x and 3x spikes), and cold-start resilience with KV-cache misses. We'll also exercise fallback policies — e.g., automatic degrade to quantized model at 90% overload. We'll capture latency, p50/p95/p99, and token throughput.
[05:55] Aaron Patel: We'll share a benchmark plan doc and runbook. Link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/lumina-poc (note: placeholder link)
[06:05] Jin Park: One question on autoscaling times. How long to scale a new instance and what is the typical latency hit?
[06:13] Samira Khan: Scaling time depends on whether it's warm or cold. Warm warm-pool scale is seconds (20-60s), cold on-demand could be 2-5 minutes depending on model size and image pull time. We use fast image layering and kernel warm start to reduce that. Caches take additional time to warm depending on your cache hit patterns.
[06:30] Eliot Rees: So for spikes we need fallback policies to avoid p99 degradation. What's common practice?
[06:37] Samira Khan: Common patterns: rate-limit non-critical routes, degrade to a smaller model for lower priority requests, and leverage stale cached responses. Also you can have queuing with headroom thresholds — e.g., allow queueing up to 200ms before switching to fallback.
[06:52] Maya Lopez: What about predictability for billing? We don't want surprise bills from burst.
[06:58] Aaron Patel: We'll provide a pricing simulator with committed monthly cost vs predicted burst spend under different spike profiles. We can also set hard caps: if burst spend would exceed X, we can fail closed or reroute to local infra.
[07:12] Jin Park: Is KV cache a first-class feature in Redwood? We've heard mixed td about 'kv cache' performance on some runtimes.
[07:20] Samira Khan: Yes KV cache is first-class. We support prefix caching and per-GPU shared KV stores. There are differences per runtime and quantization; we'll include measured cache hit latencies for your model family in the benchmark. Note: internal shorthand sometimes shows as "k v c cache" in our docs, ignore that.
[07:36] Aaron Patel: For the POC timeline proposed: 1) ingest your traces and configs (this week), 2) Redwood runs capacity sim and sends 3 commit scenarios (3 business days), 3) Lumina picks scenario and we provision dedicated reserved pool and warm burst (1-2 days), 4) Run 7-day pilot with traffic replay and live validation (7 days), 5) Wrap-up + decision. Total ~3 weeks if traces flow fast.
[08:05] Maya Lopez: That timeline works. We want the pilot to include a canary rollback plan and A/B traffic split.
[08:12] Samira Khan: We'll configure canary routing in Redwood Console — you can do percentage splits and automatic rollback based on latency/regression thresholds.
[08:20] Eliot Rees: For the canary we want to measure model quality regressions too, not just latency. Can Redwood integrate eval hooks?
[08:27] Samira Khan: Yes Redwood Optimize can evaluate prompt sets; we'll run a small evaluation suite against both primary and fallback models during the pilot and surface regressions in the console.
[08:40] Jin Park: On networking, we need VPC peering and private subnets for Dedicated. How does that affect scaling?
[08:48] Samira Khan: VPC peering and private subnets are supported, but on very rapid scale-ups you may see slightly longer provisioning due to network attach. Warm pools mitigate that. We'll run tests in your VPC during the POC.
[09:00] Maya Lopez: Security: SAML SSO for our team plus SCIM provisioning required. Also we need audit log retention for 12 months.
[09:08] Aaron Patel: We support SAML SSO and SCIM; audit retention tiers are configurable (we'll include pricing for 12 months). Also we'll send SOC 2 and dataflow diagrams.
[09:18] Eliot Rees: Practical question: how do you measure per-request cost to attribute to product lines?
[09:24] Samira Khan: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown and per-route cost. We can tag routes and export cost CSVs per team for chargeback.
[09:32] Jin Park: Great. Can you give an example commit scenario with numbers?
[09:36] Samira Khan: Sure off the cuff: for your 13B at 1200 steady rps baseline we might recommend reserving 8 A100-equivalent GPU slots with batching tuned to 4-6 concurrency per GPU. That would cover baseline. Warm burst pool + 4 GPUs for spikes to reach 2400. On-demand public burst if enabled could add 6 more GPUs transiently. We'll run exact sims with your traces.
[09:58] Aaron Patel: And cost-wise that maps to monthly commit $X (we'll fill in real numbers in the spreadsheet). The spreadsheet will show committed vs expected burst spend given historical spike profile you provide.
[10:10] Maya Lopez: One more thing: we run nightly heavy ETL scoring which generates sustained loads off-hours. Will reserved capacity be used for that or should we schedule batch runs?
[10:20] Samira Khan: You can schedule dedicated batch windows that reuse reserved capacity off-peak; Redwood supports scheduled job windows to avoid extra burst cost. We'll factor that into the cost model.
[10:30] Jin Park: Regarding fallback policy implementation — who manages rollout logic? Does Redwood control route switching?
[10:36] Samira Khan: You manage policies in the Console; we provide templates and can automate via API (rollout rules + automatic fallback). For POC we'll set suggested rules, but you keep control.
[10:46] Eliot Rees: From ML accuracy side, degrading to a smaller model has to be scoped. We'll pick 10 eval prompts and measure delta.
[10:52] Samira Khan: Sounds good. We'll run Redwood Optimize eval hooks for that.
[10:58] Aaron Patel: I'll summarize commercial options in the plan: A: Higher commit with warm bursts (best latency), B: Lower commit with on-demand public bursts (cost saver but higher cold-latency), C: Hybrid with scheduled batch reuse.
[11:12] Maya Lopez: For compliance we must avoid public bursts for certain routes. Can we tag route-level policies to enforce that?
[11:18] Samira Khan: Absolutely — route-level tags and policy enforcement in Dedicated/Private. We'll include examples.
[11:24] Jin Park: Is there an SLA for burst availability?
[11:27] Aaron Patel: Dedicated has SLA targets for capacity; public burst availability isn't SLA-backed in the same way. We'll highlight that in the doc.
[11:35] Maya Lopez: OK let's talk test plan specifics. We want ramp tests to 1.5x and 3x, steady-state periods lasting 30 mins each, plus 10 cold-start cycles to measure cache warm times.
[11:46] Samira Khan: We'll include that. Also we'd like to measure end-to-end with your frontend timeout behavior — sometimes frontends drop at 500ms. Knowing that helps set degradation thresholds.
[11:56] Eliot Rees: We'll provide frontend timeout settings.
[12:00] Aaron Patel: On observability, we'll enable distributed tracing and export payload-less traces for compliance.
[12:06] Maya Lopez: Good. Any risk flags we should know about?
[12:10] Samira Khan: A key risk is underestimating cold cache miss patterns — if your traffic has many unique user prefixes the warm pool helps. Another is large model checkpoint pulls for cold bursts. We'll highlight mitigations.
[12:24] Aaron Patel: Ok nearing the last section — admin and sign-offs. Who on your side will own the POC?
[12:30] Maya Lopez: I'll be the POC owner, Jin will handle infra, Eliot ML experiments.
[12:36] Aaron Patel: Great. We'll route the final draft to you with action items.
[12:40] Jin Park: One operational question: how do you handle multi-tenant GPUs — are customers isolated?
[12:46] Samira Khan: Redwood Dedicated provides tenant isolation via reserved pools and network isolation; on shared hosted instances we isolate at runtime but may be multi-tenant. For your compliance, Dedicated is recommended.
[12:58] Eliot Rees: Do you support mixed-precision quantization during the pilot? We want to test int8 profiles.
[13:05] Samira Khan: Yes int8/4-bit quant profiles are supported and we'll include them in the perf bench. Some kernels behave differently and may slightly change latency numbers so we'll show that in the results.
[13:18] Aaron Patel: Alright let's recap quickly and lock dates.

Recap:
- Deliverables: capacity scenarios + cost spreadsheet, benchmark plan + runbook, security packet, scheduled pilot.
- Timeline: traces by 2025-11-20, sims & scenarios by 2025-11-17, provisioning 1-2 days after scenario selection, 7-day pilot after provisioning. Target decision: end of November.
